newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU candidates pleased but some face tough talks.
newsitem.headline: EU candidates pleased but some face tough talks.

text.p: Countries tagged to be in the European Union's first eastward enlargement voiced satisfaction on Tuesday although several acknowledged they still had work ahead to meet the entry requirements.

But Romania, which along with some other countries was left out of the recommended first wave of negotiations, criticised the limit to six nations and said all candidates should start talks at the same time.
"The negotiations will be difficult," said Czech Foreign Ministry spokesman Vit Kurfuerst after receiving the news that Prague had been recommended to join talks next year.

"We all remember the negotiation process of the last group of Scandinavian countries and Austria (to join the European grouping). So we expect a difficult process -- but we expect good results," he told Reuters.

The European Commission agreed to recommend six nations for a first wave of entry talks -- Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovenia and Estonia joining Cyprus, which had already been promised membership talks.
Warsaw welcomed the acknowledgement of the effort Poles have already made towards membership.
"We feel like an enterprise that has received the approval of its auditors," said Jaroslaw Pietras, deputy minister in Poland's committee overseeing the EU membership drive.
Poland, which escaped Soviet military and economic domination only in 1989, is determined to bind itself to Western structures, but its relations with the EU have been troubled by trade disputes.

EU officials have reproached Warsaw over issues like protection of its oil and steel industries and duties on Scotch whisky. They have also urged the country to hasten the laborious process of adjusting its laws and procedures to EU standards and expressed doubts about the state of Polish agriculture, with its many small and inefficient farms.
In the tiny Baltic state of Estonia, foreign ministry spokesperson Ehtel Halliste told Reuters: "We are very happy about the decision."
Estonia, which quit the former Soviet Union in 1991 along with Latvia and Lithuania, embarked on a radical course of market reforms.
"Hungary was pleased to see another firm commitment from the Commission to enlarging the European Union," foreign ministry spokesman Gabor Horvath told Reuters.
"We are convinced that the indication that Hungary will be included in the first round of enlargement is a clear recognition that Hungary has satisfied the criteria of accession."
But he acknowledged that there would be "a few areas in which we will have to work".
Romania, Bulgaria, Latvia, Lithuania and Slovakia were left to prepare for membership at their own pace.
Romania implicitly criticised the limit of six countries, saying any enlargement in waves would be "artificial and discriminatory".

Government ministers said the EU move excluding Romania was no more than a recommendation to be confirmed later this year. But they admitted the country had to proceed with reforms to enable the economy to adapt to membership.
In a statement sent to the EU ahead of the Commission's decision at a meeting in Strasbourg, the government said all candidates should begin talks on membership at the same time.
Trade and Industry Minister Calin Popescu Tariceanu said he expected Romania would win EU membership within six to seven years.
The Commission's ruling was issued a week after NATO limited its initial eastward expansion to Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, leaving Romania on the sidelines.
Slovenia ratified its association agreement with the EU in a parliamentary vote coinciding with Brussels' decision to invite the ex-Yugoslav republic to begin full entry talks.
"This is a very important, historic decision by parliament," Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek told reporters.
"We are entering talks with a changed constitution and the association accord ratified," he said.
